result.summary: Phineus bursts into Cepheus's wedding feast with armed followers to claim Andromeda, and a massacre follows. Perseus kills many, then, outnumbered, turns the Gorgon's head on his enemies and petrifies them, including Phineus. He then returns to Argos and turns Proetus to stone.

scenes.title: Phineus bursts into the feast
scenes.summary: As Perseus tells his tale, Phineus and his band break in, turning the wedding banquet into a riot.
scenes.stakes: Perseus and Cepheus's household face an armed mob that wants to seize Andromeda.

scenes.title: Cepheus pleads; first blows
scenes.summary: Phineus threatens Perseus, Cepheus reproaches him, and Phineus hurls a spear and misses. Perseus throws it back, hits Rhoetus, and Phineus hides behind an altar.
scenes.stakes: Perseus risks death in the brawl; Phineus risks losing Andromeda.

scenes.title: The slaughter in the hall
scenes.summary: Pallas protects Perseus as the fighting spreads. Many are killed on both sides, including Athis, Lycabas, Emathion and the musician Pettalus.
scenes.stakes: Everyone in the hall risks death; Perseus fights alone against many.

scenes.title: Perseus surrounded
scenes.summary: Phineus and a thousand men surround Perseus, who backs against a pillar and fights on.
scenes.stakes: Perseus faces being overwhelmed by sheer numbers.

scenes.title: The Gorgon's head turns men to stone
scenes.summary: Perseus shows the Gorgon's head and warns friends to look away. Thescelus, Ampyx, Nileus, Eryx and about two hundred others turn to stone.
scenes.stakes: Perseus's life depends on the head; his enemies lose their lives.

scenes.title: Phineus begs and is petrified
scenes.summary: Phineus pleads for his life, and Perseus promises him a permanent monument. He turns the head on him, and Phineus becomes stone in a suppliant pose.
scenes.stakes: Phineus begs to keep his life.

scenes.title: Perseus turns Proetus to stone
scenes.summary: Perseus returns to Argos with his wife and attacks Proetus, who had seized Acrisius's citadel. The Gorgon defeats him.
scenes.stakes: Proetus risks losing the usurped citadel.

alias_notes.explanation: Patronymic style naming Perseus via his ancestor Abas.

notable_quotes.reason: Memorable image of the dying musician playing a last dirge.
Perseus's grim promise of a lasting monument to Phineus.

analysis.text: A wedding feast descends into senseless slaughter, showing how a broken promise and wounded pride lead to violence, with poetic justice in petrification.
Ovid parodies epic battle catalogues with long lists of obscure victims and gory similes, a style familiar from Homer and Virgil.

legacy.text: Perseus's use of Medusa's head recurs in the film Clash of the Titans (1981), though that film changes the story.

fun_facts.text: Ovid's battle lists give each victim a strange origin or last gesture, which makes the passage a showpiece of epic parody.

language_notes.text: Jupiter turned into 'fictitious gold' refers to Jupiter coming to Danaë as a golden shower, making Perseus his son; Phineus mocks this parentage. 'Wings' refers to Perseus's winged sandals.
The Nereids' anger and horned Ammon caused the sea monster to be sent against Andromeda; Cepheus says these, not Perseus, 'took her away' by threatening her death.
'Forsooth' is an archaic, sarcastic 'indeed'; Cepheus mocks Phineus's complaint.
'Stipulated for' means 'agreed upon as a condition': Perseus was promised Andromeda as the price for killing the monster.
'Cushion' refers to the couch on which Perseus reclined at the banquet, in the Roman dining manner.
Gods of hospitality: Jove was protector of guests and hosts, so violence at a banquet broke sacred obligations. Cepheus is Perseus' host and father-in-law.
"Her brother": Pallas (Minerva) and Perseus share the father Jove, so she calls him brother, in a loose sense.
Billet: a thick piece of firewood, here taken from the burning altar and used as a club.
Falchion: a short, slightly curved sword. This is the blade Perseus used to kill Medusa.
"Grandson of Acrisius": a patronymic for Perseus, whose mother Danaë was Acrisius' daughter.
"Son of Iapetus": the musician is addressed in the second person, but the name Iapetus is unusual; the victim is named Pettalus in the next sentence.
Stygian ghosts: the dead of the underworld, named for the river Styx.
"Descendant of Abas": Perseus, whose ancestor Abas was a king of Argos. Not to be confused with the Abas who kills Pelates.
Sagacious: wise and perceptive; here it sets up the irony of a seer who failed to foresee his own death.
Bellona was the Roman goddess of war; here she stands for the battle itself, which turns the wedding hall into a bloody field.
Cyllenian falchion: the curved sword Perseus got from Mercury, who was born on Mount Cyllene. A falchion is a broad, curved blade.
"Seek assistance from an enemy" means Perseus will use the Gorgon's head, which is hostile to everyone, as his ally. "Miracles" is Thescelus's scornful word for it.
The seven-mouthed Nile refers to the seven branches of the Nile delta. Nileus claims the river god as his father, which the narrator says is false.
"Rebuked them" means Eryx scolded his frozen comrades. The footnote marker [21] belongs to the translator, not to Ovid.
The sentence is muddled. It means Aconteus, who fought for Perseus, looked at the Gorgon and was turned to stone, though he did not deserve it like the others.
"Stone-making face" means Medusa's severed head, which Perseus holds and which turns anyone who looks at it to stone.
Phineus claims priority: he was betrothed to Andromeda first, while Perseus's claim rests on rescuing her from the sea monster.
"Boon" means a favor or gift; "craven" means cowardly.
"Daughter of Phorcys" is Medusa, one of the Gorgons, whose father was the sea god Phorcys.
"Descendant of Abas" is Perseus, whose grandfather Acrisius was a descendant of Abas, an earlier king of Argos.
Prœtus had driven out his twin brother Acrisius and seized Argos. Perseus, Acrisius's grandson, now comes to restore the family's rule.

context_notes.text: Phineus is Cepheus's brother and Andromeda's uncle and betrothed. Perseus has just told of killing Medusa and rescuing Andromeda from the sea monster.
An altar was a place of sanctuary, so Phineus's refuge there made violence against him sacrilegious.
Ganges is the great river of India. Nymph mothers like Limnate are typical of mythic heroes born from rivers.
Semiramis was the legendary Assyrian queen of Babylon, famed for her power and conquests.
Ceres was goddess of grain and harvest. Her priests wore white fillets, headbands marking sacred office.
The Nasamonians were a Libyan people of North Africa, so Dorylas' wealth is in that region.
Molpeus and Ethemon are fighters from distant lands, Chaonia in Epirus and Nabathæa in Arabia. Phineus has gathered a wide, mixed force.
Perseus carries the head of Medusa, the Gorgon. Anyone who looks at it turns to stone, so he warns his friends to turn away.
Andromeda is Perseus's wife and Phineus's former betrothed. Her father Cepheus is the "father-in-law" whose house will display the statue.

literary_notes.text: The sudden uproar at the feast is compared to winds whipping a calm sea into waves, conveying how quickly peace turns to violence.
Cepheus's string of questions voices outrage and shames Phineus before the guests, and prepares his argument about ingratitude.
The narrator's exclamation 'how unworthily!' breaks in with moral judgment, showing the altar's sanctity abused to shield a wicked man.
The spear meant for Phineus kills Rhœtus instead, and the dying man's blood stains the feast tables, grimly reversing the banquet setting.
The lavish catalogue of Athis' beauty, dress and ornaments makes his sudden death more pitiable and shows Ovid's taste for ornate description.
Lycabas dying on his friend's body, finding "consolation" in shared death, gives a moment of tenderness amid the carnage.
Ammon's boxing skill is mocked: it is useless against swords, a wry aside undercutting the warrior's pride.
The dying musician plays his last notes on the lyre, a poignant touch contrasting art and violence.
Comparing Pettalus' fall to a slaughtered bullock reduces the man to an animal victim, stressing the brutality of the fight.
Abas' corpse hanging from the doorpost by a pinned hand turns death into a grim spectacle, typical of this epic battle.
Æthion, a seer, is undone by a false omen, so his foresight fails him in the end.
Darts flying thicker than winter hail exaggerate the volume of missiles, making Perseus's peril vivid.
Perseus, pulled between two foes, is compared to a tiger hesitating between two herds. This shows the pressure on him and his fierce, predatory energy.
Thescelus mocks the "miracles" and is frozen mid-throw. His scorn is answered at once, and he becomes a statue in the pose of his threat.
Nileus has just boasted that Perseus will die proud of being killed by him. Instead his half-open mouth is frozen, and his boast goes unfinished.
Perseus's "gift" of a permanent monument is a cruel joke: Phineus is spared weapons but will be fixed in stone and displayed to the wife he wanted.
The moisture of his eyes hardening into stone makes the transformation physical, as the living body turns to rock bit by bit.
The frozen details of timid face, pleading expression and hanging hands show the petrified Phineus fixed forever in his cowardly pose.
